edition_identity_boundary.evidence: The current later editorial family exposes 40 chapters while the separately identified 1928 first standalone edition exposes 41 chapters. This structural difference is sufficient to prohibit collapsing the two public routes into one edition/text identity, but it is not by itself a byte-level comparison or proof of every textual difference.
edition_identity_boundary.rule: Do not infer FantLab analyzer-input identity from title, authorship, publication history, chapter count, bibliographic compatibility, or public availability. Each edition/transcription family requires its own immutable literary-text identity before diagnostics.

legal_boundary.evidence: Russian Wikisource marks both retained original-Russian work surfaces public domain. Candidate scope is the literary body only; no source prose, scan bytes, translation, derivative work, or later editorial apparatus is committed.

diversity.reason_selected: This adds a legally usable long coauthored 20th-century candidate, preserves a documented first-edition versus later-editorial-family split, and exposes a future author-voice methodological case where single-author attribution assumptions are unsafe.

reasons: FantLab reports 572,654 characters and 80,203 words for its 17 September 2022 analysis, above the 300,000-character calibration threshold.
Russian Wikisource provides explicit public-domain evidence and stable work-index locators for two distinct bibliographic/text families.
The later family has 40 visible chapters while the first standalone 1928 family has 41, so Scriptorium must not flatten them into one edition identity.
Neither public literary body is fully revision-pinned under a deterministic extraction/composition contract with composite digests.
FantLab does not disclose the edition or immutable bytes of the text uploaded for its 2022 analysis.
